title: Is Egypt Safe for Solo Female Travellers? Honest Advice
excerpt: What the UK, US and Canadian governments say about Egypt today, what harassment looks like, and dress, transport and tour advice for women travelling alone.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

The quick answer

Many women travel Egypt alone, and it can be done well, but nobody can honestly call it risk-free. As of 8 November 2026, the UK, US and Canadian governments all advise caution in Egypt because of terrorism and all name areas to avoid (North Sinai, the Libyan border region and parts of the Western Desert); none of them advises women against travelling to the main Nile Valley tourist route. The UK and Canadian advice both address harassment, and the UK advises women travelling alone to take care, particularly at night. In practice, much of the work is managing attention: how you dress, the rhythm of your days and a flat, final "no". Women-only Metro cars, app-based taxis, daylight site visits and a confirmed small group turn "travelling alone" into "travelling with options".

Check current UK government travel advice for Egypt before making your arrangements; advice can change.

Two reactions meet a woman who says she is travelling Egypt alone. The first is the news version, where the country is one unresolved headline; the second is the brochure version, where everything is sunset-coloured and effortless. Neither helps with planning. This guide sits between them. It sets out what the governments say today, what harassment typically looks like here, how to dress and move, where to sleep, who to call when something happens, and the tour types that make solo days easier. It is written by the team behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure platform.

What the governments say, as of 8 November 2026

Start with the official picture, because it changes and because your insurance may depend on it. The FCDO states that your travel insurance could be invalidated if you travel against its advice.

Government What it says about Egypt overall What it says about women
UK: FCDO Egypt travel advice (updated 27 October 2026) Advises against all travel to North Sinai and within 20 km of the Libyan border, and against all but essential travel to parts of South Sinai and much of the desert west of the Nile Valley, with named exceptions such as Siwa town, Bahariya and the White and Black Deserts. Warns that terrorists are likely to try to carry out attacks. Describes the crime rate as generally low Advises women travelling alone to take care, particularly at night. Reports that most reported sexual assaults have been in Red Sea tourist resorts, and that some victims have been discouraged by hotel staff from going to the police
US: State Department Egypt advisory Level 2, "Exercise Increased Caution", as reported in 2026 and restated in US Embassy Cairo alerts of March and April 2026. Do not travel to Northern and Middle Sinai or parts of the Western Desert Read the full advisory for its current wording on women travellers
Canada: Travel advice and advisories for Egypt (page dated 26 May 2026) A high degree of caution overall, with a terrorism threat; avoid all travel to North Sinai, near the Libyan border and in parts of the Western Desert Warns that women, especially foreigners, often face unwanted attention, harassment and verbal abuse, more so on public holidays; advises against sitting in the front seat of taxis; flags a serious risk of sexual assault at demonstrations; notes women-only Metro cars; advises conservative dress

Read these as a map of the risk, not a verdict. "Not named" does not mean "no risk", and the wording above will change, so read your own government's page in the week you book.

The honest picture: what solo female travel in Egypt is like

Harassment is mostly passive, and sometimes it is not. Typically it is staring: long, unapologetic and constant. Then comments, hisses and "welcome to Egypt" openers that go on a beat too long. Vendors and self-appointed guides escalate persistence rather than menace: photo requests, "just one shop", walk-with-you offers that become hard to shake. Less often, and not unknown, is unwanted physical attention in crowds or from someone you have already met. The UK and Canadian advice both treat this seriously, and so should any traveller. Each of these has a defusal (a flat tone, public space, moving on), and most travellers find them easier to handle on day three than on day one.

Where you are changes how it feels. The classic Cairo, Luxor and Aswan corridor is used to foreign women travelling; villages and off-path towns tend to be friendlier in spirit and stricter in dress expectations. One finding belongs in an honest guide even though tourism marketing leaves it out: the UK government reports that most reported sexual assaults in Egypt have been in Red Sea tourist resorts, and that some victims have been discouraged from reporting. Read that not as "avoid Egypt" but as "choose your accommodation and excursion staff as carefully as you choose your sights".

Dress and presence: what changes how you are treated

Dress modestly and loosely, with shoulders and knees covered. The FCDO advises modest dress, particularly in rural areas, mosques and markets, and notes that dress which ignores local codes can cause more offence during Ramadan. This is not about apologising for existing; it is about buying comfort. Loose linen trousers, long skirts, tunic tops and a scarf for mosque visits will draw less attention than tight or revealing clothes, and they are cooler than bare skin in the sun anyway. The Canadian advice goes further, suggesting conservative dress with longer sleeves and hemlines; most visitors settle somewhere in between.

Presence does the rest. Sunglasses cut the eye-contact loop that invites commentary. "La, shukran" (no, thank you), delivered flat and once, ends more conversations than any speech; engagement is what vendors read as interest. Headphones are a social forcefield on Metro platforms and in bazaars. None of this guarantees silence, but together it can turn the daily attention into background noise.

Getting around safely: Metro, taxis, trains and night

App-based transport and daylight rhythms solve much of the transport question. Uber and Careem work in Cairo; check coverage in the other cities before relying on them. The fare is shown before you get in, the route is tracked, and trips can be shared with someone at home. The FCDO's advice to take care when alone at night is a sensible rule to organise a day around: sites early, dinner early, app taxis after dark, and no long night drives outside cities. In a taxi or app car, the Canadian advice is not to sit in the front seat.

The Cairo Metro is fast and costs a fraction of a euro (EGP 10 to 20 a ride, about €0.17 to €0.33 at EGP 60 to the euro on 8 November 2026), and it has women-only cars: the fourth and fifth, in the middle of the train, with the fifth reported to open to everyone after 21:00. Look for the signage on the platform. They are optional, since you may ride any car, but at rush hour many women find them calmer. The Metro runs from about 5am to midnight. On trains between cities, sit near families, and on the overnight sleeper choose your cabin according to your own comfort rather than the cheapest option.

If something happens: who to call

Save these before you fly: tourist police 126 (built for visitors: scams, harassment, theft), police 122, ambulance 123, fire 180. The FCDO adds that a crime not reported before you leave Egypt is difficult to prosecute later, and that is one reason to report what deserves reporting: touching, following, persistent intrusion after a clear no. Tourist police officers are posted at major sites and tourist areas. On a Sawa departure there is also a WhatsApp line, +20 109 284 7613, answered 24/7 while your tour is running, so someone on the Sawa side can help the same day. Given the UK's finding that victims have been discouraged from reporting, do not let anyone talk you out of it.

Hotel choice: where women sleep well

Choose in this order: area, desk, reviews. Area first: central areas with restaurants, pharmacies and other travellers (Downtown and Zamalek are common bases in Cairo) beat dark driveways. Desk second: a 24-hour reception changes what a late train arrival means. Reviews third, and not for the breakfast: search them for solo women's mentions, and read the negative ones for how management behaves when a guest reports a problem. That last point matters because of the UK finding about discouraged reporting; staff behaviour belongs on your checklist.

The solo-room premium is real at many hotels, as is the single-supplement trap on tours. Hostels skip both and add company; small family-run hotels often price single rooms fairly. Book the first night's airport pickup through the hotel, and let the first evening be an easy one.

Practical tips

Habits worth building

  • Live on daylight rhythm. Sites at opening, lunch late, dinner early, app taxi home. Many sites close by late afternoon anyway.
  • Book the first night's airport pickup through your hotel. The arrival taxi is the one negotiation you do not want jet-lagged.
  • Carry small Egyptian pound notes for toilets, tea and tips; cards are not accepted everywhere.
  • Build the check-in habit. Share your app trips and send a message each day to someone at home.
  • Define your leave signal. Decide in advance what behaviour ends a conversation or a visit; you will enforce it better for having decided it calmly.
  • Dress for the site, not the photograph. The loose-linen uniform photographs well anyway.
  • Avoid demonstrations and large crowds, which the Canadian advice singles out for women.

Common mistakes

  • Treating all attention as danger. Most of it is commerce, and overreacting exhausts you before the real signals arrive. The reverse mistake is ignoring a pattern that is not commerce.
  • Under-drinking water. Dehydration headaches ruin judgement; carry bottled water.
  • Following a "helpful" stranger without agreeing a price first.
  • Booking non-refundable extras before a trip is confirmed.
  • Skipping the police report when something real happens.

The honest downsides, in one place: the attention is daily, some days it lands badly, and you will occasionally be spoken over or quoted tourist prices for fruit. Weigh that against sites like Karnak at opening and a Nile felucca at sunset.

The short version

Egypt asks women to be deliberate rather than fearless. Governments advise caution and warn about harassment; the main tourist route is outside the areas they tell you to avoid. Dress modestly and loosely, move by app, keep nights short, choose hotels on desk and reviews, and put a guide or a confirmed small group around the remote legs. Save the numbers: tourist police 126, police 122, ambulance 123. Then see the forming departures.

faq.q: Is Egypt safe for a woman travelling alone?
faq.a: Many women do it, with care, but no destination is risk-free. The UK, US and Canadian governments advise caution in Egypt and name areas to avoid; the UK advises women travelling alone to take care, particularly at night, and the UK and Canada both warn about harassment. Dress modestly, move by app, keep evenings early and take a guide or group for the remote legs. Read your own government's advice in the week you book.

faq.q: What's the best way for a woman to tour Egypt alone?
faq.a: A confirmed small group is a good ratio of company to freedom: shared departures pool you with other travellers (on Sawa, four to eight people, with WhatsApp answered 24/7 while your tour is running). A private guide suits travellers who want full control, and some operators run women-only departures. Use day tours for the logistics-heavy sights and go independently for the walkable middle.

faq.q: What should women wear in Egypt?
faq.a: Loose, breathable clothing with shoulders and knees covered, such as linen trousers, midi skirts and tunic tops, plus a scarf for mosques. The FCDO advises modest dress, particularly in rural areas, mosques and markets, and during Ramadan. It is less about rules and more about friction: covered travellers tend to attract less attention.

faq.q: Is Cairo safe for a solo woman at night?
faq.a: The UK advice is for women travelling alone to take care, particularly at night. In practice, many women arrange dinner in a central area and take an app car home, and avoid quiet side streets, unlicensed taxis and long walks late. Plan the evening before dark and let the app do the driving.

faq.q: Are there women-only tours in Egypt, and can I request a female guide?
faq.a: Some operators offer women-only departures, though dates are limited. Sawa's tours are fixed products run as mixed groups of up to eight, so Sawa cannot promise a female guide or a women-only departure.

faq.q: What should I do if I'm harassed in Egypt?
faq.a: Move to a public, populated space, say "la" flatly and keep walking, and report what deserves reporting (touching, following, persistence after a clear no) to the tourist police on 126 or at a site kiosk. Note the place and time and tell your hotel or guide. If you are on a Sawa departure, message the WhatsApp line at +20 109 284 7613.
